newsitem.title: USA: Ford files for Hertz initial public offering.
newsitem.headline: Ford files for Hertz initial public offering.

text.p: Ford Motor Co., aiming to unlock more of the value tied up in its non-automotive assets, said Friday it plans to sell less than 20 percent of its Hertz Corp. car rental unit in an initial public offering.

Ford said the offering, which had been long expected, will involve newly issued shares of Hertz common stock. A registration statement for the offering was filed Friday with the Securities and Exchange Commission in Washington.
The transaction will mark the end of Ford's three-year ownership of 100 percent of Hertz, which claims to be the world's largest car rental concern.

Ford first invested in the Park Ridge, N.J.,-based car rental giant in 1987 to gain a captive customer for its vehicles. The strategy, also pursued by General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp., allowed the automaker to keep its factories running during the early 1990s recession, but barely used rental cars soon lured buyers away from new cars.
Analysts said Friday that Hertz as a whole is worth up to $3 billion, meaning that Ford could gain up to $600 million in cash in the 20 percent offering.
"The market has an eppetite for rental car companies and Hertz is the best of the bunch," said Bear, Stearns & Co. analyst Nicholas Lobocarro. "It makes sense for them to take some cash out now."

Unlike the financial problems encountered by many of its competitors in recent years, Hertz has posted record earnings for four years in a row, earning $159 million on revenues of $3.7 billion in 1996. In 1995, Hertz earned $105 million on revenues of $3.4 billion.

While Hertz outranks all competitors in worldwide revenues and fleet size, Auto Rental News ranks the company's 300,000-vehicle U.S. fleet below that of St. Louis-based Enterprise Rent-A-Car -- a title Hertz disputes.

Ford named J.P. Morgan & Co Inc. as the lead underwriter for the Hertz offering, dealing another blow to Goldman Sachs & Co., Ford's longtime lead investment bank. J.P. Morgan was the lead underwriter for an initial offering in Ford's Associates First Capital Corp. unit last year.

Ford spokesman Christian Vinyard said pricing of the Hertz shares is at least "several weeks" away. By comparison, Ford filed for the Associates offering in February 1996, and the shares were not priced until early May.

Vinyard said Ford is keeping more than 80 percent of Hertz so it can continue to consolidate Hertz' earnings on its books for tax purposes. Asked if Ford may sell more of its stake at a later date, he said that was "very premature to even think about right now."

Dean Witter analyst Ronald Glantz, said he believes it is ultimately a good idea for Ford to divest the remainder of Hertz. "Owning your own captive car company makes it easy to make strategic errors," he said.

Ford Vice Chairman Ed Hagenlocker said ingestor interest in the rental car industry prompted Ford's action. "We believe that it is now in the best interest of our shareholders to consider an initial public offering of Hertz," he said in a statement.
The deal also will make Hertz the sixth major U.S. car rental agency to undergo an ownership change since 1994.

Ford sold its interest in Budget Rent a Car Corp. to Fort Lauderdale, Fla.-based Team Rental Group Inc. for $350 million in January. General Motors Corp sold its 29 percent stake in Avis Inc. to HFS Inc., a New Jersey-based hotel and real estate concern.

Also in February, investor Wayne Huizenga's Republic Industries Inc. bought National Car Rental System Inc. for $600 million, adding to its purchase last year of Alamo Rent-A-Car Inc. The two firms are also expected to provide Huizenga's growing auto dealership holdings with an an ample supply of late-model used cars.
Chrysler Corp. also is seeking a buyer for its Dollar and Thrifty car rental units.
